202	Running Title: Social Media May Cause Emergent SARMs Abuse by Athletes        IP
203	                                                                         R
204	Abstract                                                      SC
205	Objectives:                                             U
206	                                             AN
207	Selective Androgen Receptor Modulators (SARMs) social media interest is at an all-time high.
208	
209	The aim of this study is to analyze the: (1) quality; (2) educational content; and (3) reliability of
210	                                       M
211	the most relevant YouTube videos on SARMs to explain growing SARMs abuse by recreational
212	
213	and professional athletes.     D
214	Methods:             TE
215	           EP
216	‘SARMs’ was queried (November 28, 2021) through the YouTube video library. The top 100
217	
218	videos filtered by relevance were categorized by source, type of content, educational quality by
219	     C
220	Global Quality Score (GQS), reliability by Journal of American Medicine Association (JAMA)
221	
222	AC
223	criteria, YouTube tags, attitude towards SARMs use, and whether the video provided specific
224	
225	support on how to use SARMs. For all outcome variables, descriptive statistics and comparison
226	
227	among source types and category types were performed.
228	
229	Results:
230	 Mean JAMA score was 1.6 ± 0.7 out of 4. Mean GQS score was 2.5 ± 1.1 out of 5. Patient
231	
232	videos were of lower educational quality than athletic trainer videos (GQS: 2.11 ± 0.95 vs. 2.95
233	
234	± 1.00, p < 0.01), and videos categorized as user experience were of lower educational quality
235	
236	than videos categorized as general SARMs information (GQS: 1.92 ± 0.90 vs. 2.72 ± 1.07, p <
237	
238	0.05). User experience and dosing recommendation videos were statistically significantly more
239	                                                                                  T
240	                                                                          IP
241	positive in attitude than both general SARMs information and SARMS vs. other PEDs.
242	
243	Conclusion:                                                          R
244	                                                           SC
245	Quality, content, and reliability of SARMs YouTube videos was low. Social media likely causes
246	
247	SARMs abuse through disseminating biased SARMs misinformation. These results serve to
248	                                                     U
249	educate public health oversight bodies, healthcare providers, and sports team members to better
250	                                           AN
251	identify signs of SARMs abuse, and promote discussion to discourage SARMs abuse.
252	
253	
254	                                     M
255	                             D
256	Keywords: Performance enhancing drugs, Drug Abuse, Substance use disorder, Selective
257	
258	
259	                    TE
260	Androgen Receptor Modulators, YouTube, Social media, Athletes
261	
262	
263	
264	          EP
265	Data Availability Statement:
266	
267	    C
268	The data that support the findings of this study are available from the corresponding author, NV,
269	
270	AC
271	upon reasonable request.
272	 Introduction
273	
274	Selective Androgen Receptor Modulators (SARMs) are a class of performance enhancing drugs
275	
276	(PEDs) that act as androgen receptor ligands that achieve tissue-selective activation of
277	
278	androgenic signaling. The non-steroidal forms of SARMs were discovered in the late 1990s,
279	
280	                                                                                   T
281	originally demonstrating potential to treat muscle wasting in patients with cancer, osteoporosis,
282	
283	                                                                            IP
284	advanced age, and other chronic illnesses [1]. The potential to slow the functional decline of
285	
286	
287	                                                                      R
288	older individuals using targeted androgen signaling has led to the development of non-steroidal
289	
290	
291	                                                            SC
292	SARMs from nearly all major pharmaceutical companies [2]. Clinical trials, in vivo, and in vitro
293	
294	studies suggest that SARMs can build muscle mass, much like androgenic-anabolic steroids [3-
295	
296	                                                      U
297	7]. Athletes and social media influences use this literature to justify SARMs use and promote
298	
299	                                            AN
300	SARMs on social media. However, SARMs may cause adverse effects, such as liver injury and
301	
302	acute myocarditis, and SARMs abuse should be recognized as a substance use disorder [8-14].
303	
304	                                     M
305	                              D
306	SARMs, like other PEDs, provide unfair advantages in sports activities, and SARMs abuse is
307	
308	
309	                    TE
310	rampant at the professional level. Between 2016 and 2019, the World Anti-Doping Agency
311	
312	(WADA) saw a 4-times increase in the number of SARM positive results in failed drug tests for
313	
314	          EP
315	professional sporting events worldwide [15-18]. Although the National College Athletic
316	
317	Association (NCAA) in the USA does not provide data on their drug testing results, they
318	    C
319	explicitly added SARMs to their banned substances list in 2015 [19]. Many reports of collegiate-
320	AC
321	related SARMs-use have appeared in the news and social media since then. In a 2005 U.S.
322	
323	Government hearing titled ‘Steroid Use in Sports,’ the US House of Representatives described a
324	
325	‘trickle-down effect’ on youth from professional athletes and teams [20]. Thus, young
326	
327	impressionable athletes are more likely to abuse SARMs if their favorite athletes and social
328	 media influencers abuse SARMs. In a cross-sectional randomized response technique survey,
329	
330	2.7% of young male gym-goers (N = 2264, 24 ± 6 years) reported SARMs use, and 9% reported
331	
332	using anabolic androgenic steroids [21]. Illegal substance use is commonly underreported, and
333	
334	Google Search trends analytics indicate that SARMs’ interest is rapidly increasing, and at an all-
335	
336	time high [22]. Thus, true athlete and gym-goer SARMs use prevalence is likely higher than
337	                                                                                   T
338	previously reported (>2.7%). [21]
339	                                                                            IP
340	                                                                       R
341	                                                            SC
342	In the USA, SARMs are classified as research chemicals that can be legally bought and sold
343	
344	online; however, marketing SARMs for human consumption is illegal by law. Ironically,
345	
346	                                                       U
347	numerous YouTube videos support consumption and describe different ways to properly dose
348	
349	
350	                                            AN
351	and cycle SARMs, while hiding behind disclaimers of ‘for entertainment purposes only.’ The top
352	
353	100 keyword tagged ‘SARMs’ videos on YouTube sorted by relevance add up to over
354	
355	                                      M
356	14,000,000 views. Hahamyan et al. [2022] noted that prior to the popular video sharing platform
357	
358	
359	                              D
360	TikTok ban of SARMs-related keywords, videos tagged with keyword SARMs totaled more than
361	
362	
363	                    TE
364	115 million views [23]. The paucity of clinical research on safe dosing for SARMs and
365	
366	respective side effects in recreational use suggest users and athletes turn to anecdotal evidence
367	
368	          EP
369	from online forums and now YouTube videos for guidance [22, 24].
370	
371	
372	    C
373	Alarmingly, YouTube content creators can post videos without review. Thus, YouTube can be a
374	
375	AC
376	source of widespread and readily available health misinformation, including celebratory/do-it-
377	
378	yourself videos on SARMs use. In fact, over 93% of adults in the United States use the internet,
379	
380	and 8 in 10 online inquiries for health or medical information start at a generic search engine [25,
381	
382	26]. Many patients/viewers feel that online medical information is the ‘same as’ or ‘better than’
383	 information from their doctors [27]. Clearly, to understand SARMs abuse, growing social media
384	
385	content must be analyzed.
386	
387	
388	
389	The aim of this study is to analyze the: (1) quality; (2) educational content; and (3) reliability of
390	
391	the most relevant YouTube videos on SARMs to explain growing SARMs abuse by recreational
392	                                                                                      T
393	                                                                              IP
394	and professional sports athletes. Since YouTube video content is not subject to review before
395	
396	being published, the authors hypothesized that the video quality and reliability would be low, and
397	                                                                         R
398	                                                              SC
399	the educational content would be limited with a bias towards SARMs use.
400	
401	
402	Materials and Methods
403	
404	Search/Analysis Strategy
405	                                                        U
406	                                             AN
407	On November 28th, 2021, a cross-sectional analysis of the YouTube video library was
408	
409	performed. The term ‘SARMs’ was queried on YouTube. The first 100 videos sorted by
410	                                       M
411	relevance were recorded. A web scraper was coded using the Beautiful Soup and Selenium
412	
413	                               D
414	Python libraries to extract characteristics from the videos. Because these extracted characteristics
415	
416	                     TE
417	from YouTube are publicly available, it fulfills criteria for Institutional Review Board (IRB)
418	
419	exemption, so approval and consent was not required.
420	          EP
421	     C
422	Extracted Characteristics
423	
424	
425	AC
426	The following variables were recorded for each video: (1) title; (2) video duration (minutes); (3)
427	
428	number of views; (4) days since upload; (5) channel name; (6) number of comments; (7) video
429	
430	tags (descriptive keywords assigned to the video upon upload); (8) view ratio (views/day); (9)
431	
432	subscriber count; (10) number of likes; (11) number of dislikes; (12) like ratio (number of likes *
433	
434	100)/(number of likes + number of dislikes); and (13) Video Power Index (VPI). VPI is defined
435	 as (like ratio * view ratio / 100) and has been characterized in prior literature as a quantitative
436	
437	measure of video popularity [28-30]. Unique case-insensitive tags were recorded for the 100
438	
439	videos. Analysis was then restricted to tags that appeared in 4+ videos, and similar tags were
440	
441	then combined into relevant categories. These tag categories were then used for frequency
442	
443	analysis and were included in multivariate regressions.
444	                                                                                      T
445	Video Categorization
446	                                                                              IP
447	                                                                         R
448	                                                              SC
449	Two reviewing authors independently reviewed and analyzed all 100 videos. Any discrepancies
450	
451	of subjective measures were resolved by discussion between the two reviewing authors to remain
452	
453	uniform.                                                U
454	                                             AN
455	Videos were classified based on upload source into the following categories: (1) physician, (2)
456	
457	                                       M
458	non-physician, (3) academic, (4) athletic trainer, (5) commercial, and (6) patient. ‘Physician’
459	
460	videos were uploaded by a physician with an MD or DO degree; ‘nonphysician’ videos were
461	                               D
462	                     TE
463	uploaded by non-physician healthcare providers; ‘academic’ videos were uploaded by authors
464	
465	with non-clinical health science credentials and non-clinical authors affiliated with research
466	
467	           EP
468	groups or universities; ‘athletic trainer’ videos were uploaded by individuals with any athletic
469	
470	training or coaching credentials; commercial videos were uploaded by a company or
471	     C
472	organization rather than an individual; ‘patient’ videos were uploaded by SARMs users not
473	
474	AC
475	previously described, or any other individual discussing SARMs without any qualifications.
476	
477	Upon upload source categorization, no videos were labeled as ‘nonphysician’ or ‘academic’ and
478	
479	these source categories were removed from results reporting and further analyses.
480	 Videos were also categorized based on their content into the following categories: (1) User
481	
482	Experience, (2) Usage Recommendations, (3) SARMs vs. other PEDs, (4) General SARMs
483	
484	Information, and (5) SARMs Purchasing and Sourcing. Although many of the videos overlapped
485	
486	in content, the category selected for each video reflected a significant majority of the content
487	
488	discussed.
489	                                                                                    T
490	Video Quality and Content
491	                                                                               IP
492	                                                                          R
493	                                                              SC
494	Video quality and reliability was measured using four Journal of the American Medical
495	
496	Association (JAMA) criteria. A single point was assigned for the presence of each criterion (i.e.,
497	
498	                                                         U
499	Authorship, Attribution, Currency, and Disclosure) creating a JAMA benchmark score between 0
500	
501	
502	                                              AN
503	and 4 [31]. Authorship describes whether the authors and/or contributors provide their
504	
505	affiliations and relevant credentials. Attribution defines whether the video properly cites and lists
506	
507	                                       M
508	relevant sources. Currency describes whether the dates that the video was posted and updated are
509	
510	
511	                               D
512	indicated. Disclosure seeks to identify whether the channel and/or contributors disclose relevant
513	
514	
515	                     TE
516	sponsors, conflicts of interest, or other support. These criteria have been used to define the
517	
518	reliability of online resources in a variety of clinical topics [28-30, 32, 33].
519	
520	          EP
521	Video educational content was also subjectively measured using the Global Quality Score
522	     C
523	(GQS). The GQS utilizes a five-point Likert scale to describe how educational or useful a video
524	
525	AC
526	is for a viewer [34]. A score of one describes the video to be of poor quality and unlikely to be
527	
528	useful for viewer education, while a score of five describes the video to be of excellent quality
529	
530	and flow and highly useful to viewers. Scores of two through four represent a gradient between
531	
532	the extremes. The reviewing authors independently scored each video and averaged the results.
533	 Specific to the topic of SARMs, two unique content scores were recorded to identify overall
534	
535	sentiment and the extent of educational information provided on these PEDs. The overall attitude
536	
537	scale measures whether the video held a positive (1), neutral (0), or negative (-1) attitude on the
538	
539	use of SARMs. Videos that support SARMs use were scored positive, and videos that discourage
540	                                                                                    T
541	                                                                             IP
542	SARMs use were scored negative. Videos that discussed the harms and potential benefits of
543	
544	SARMs use, without supporting/discouraging use were scored neutral. The specific support scale
545	                                                                        R
546	                                                             SC
547	utilizes a binary scale to indicate whether a video provides specific support on how to use
548	
549	SARMs properly. Specific support includes information on the length of a PED cycle, dosing,
550	
551	                                                       U
552	post-cycle therapy, and/or including various concomitant supplements. Because SARMs are not
553	
554

Social Media May Cause Emergent SARMs Abuse by Athletes: A Content Quality Analysis

of the Most Popular YouTube Videos                                                    T
Running Title: Social Media May Cause Emergent SARMs Abuse by Athletes        IP
                                                                         R
Abstract                                                      SC
Objectives:                                             U
                                             AN
Selective Androgen Receptor Modulators (SARMs) social media interest is at an all-time high.

The aim of this study is to analyze the: (1) quality; (2) educational content; and (3) reliability of
                                       M
the most relevant YouTube videos on SARMs to explain growing SARMs abuse by recreational

and professional athletes.     D
Methods:             TE
           EP
‘SARMs’ was queried (November 28, 2021) through the YouTube video library. The top 100

videos filtered by relevance were categorized by source, type of content, educational quality by
     C
Global Quality Score (GQS), reliability by Journal of American Medicine Association (JAMA)

AC
criteria, YouTube tags, attitude towards SARMs use, and whether the video provided specific

support on how to use SARMs. For all outcome variables, descriptive statistics and comparison

among source types and category types were performed.

Results:
 Mean JAMA score was 1.6 ± 0.7 out of 4. Mean GQS score was 2.5 ± 1.1 out of 5. Patient

videos were of lower educational quality than athletic trainer videos (GQS: 2.11 ± 0.95 vs. 2.95

± 1.00, p < 0.01), and videos categorized as user experience were of lower educational quality

than videos categorized as general SARMs information (GQS: 1.92 ± 0.90 vs. 2.72 ± 1.07, p <

0.05). User experience and dosing recommendation videos were statistically significantly more
                                                                                  T
                                                                          IP
positive in attitude than both general SARMs information and SARMS vs. other PEDs.

Conclusion:                                                          R
                                                           SC
Quality, content, and reliability of SARMs YouTube videos was low. Social media likely causes

SARMs abuse through disseminating biased SARMs misinformation. These results serve to
                                                     U
educate public health oversight bodies, healthcare providers, and sports team members to better
                                           AN
identify signs of SARMs abuse, and promote discussion to discourage SARMs abuse.


                                     M
                             D
Keywords: Performance enhancing drugs, Drug Abuse, Substance use disorder, Selective


                    TE
Androgen Receptor Modulators, YouTube, Social media, Athletes



          EP
Data Availability Statement:

    C
The data that support the findings of this study are available from the corresponding author, NV,

AC
upon reasonable request.
 Introduction

Selective Androgen Receptor Modulators (SARMs) are a class of performance enhancing drugs

(PEDs) that act as androgen receptor ligands that achieve tissue-selective activation of

androgenic signaling. The non-steroidal forms of SARMs were discovered in the late 1990s,

                                                                                   T
originally demonstrating potential to treat muscle wasting in patients with cancer, osteoporosis,

                                                                            IP
advanced age, and other chronic illnesses [1]. The potential to slow the functional decline of


                                                                      R
older individuals using targeted androgen signaling has led to the development of non-steroidal


                                                            SC
SARMs from nearly all major pharmaceutical companies [2]. Clinical trials, in vivo, and in vitro

studies suggest that SARMs can build muscle mass, much like androgenic-anabolic steroids [3-

                                                      U
7]. Athletes and social media influences use this literature to justify SARMs use and promote

                                            AN
SARMs on social media. However, SARMs may cause adverse effects, such as liver injury and

acute myocarditis, and SARMs abuse should be recognized as a substance use disorder [8-14].

                                     M
                              D
SARMs, like other PEDs, provide unfair advantages in sports activities, and SARMs abuse is


                    TE
rampant at the professional level. Between 2016 and 2019, the World Anti-Doping Agency

(WADA) saw a 4-times increase in the number of SARM positive results in failed drug tests for

          EP
professional sporting events worldwide [15-18]. Although the National College Athletic

Association (NCAA) in the USA does not provide data on their drug testing results, they
    C
explicitly added SARMs to their banned substances list in 2015 [19]. Many reports of collegiate-
AC
related SARMs-use have appeared in the news and social media since then. In a 2005 U.S.

Government hearing titled ‘Steroid Use in Sports,’ the US House of Representatives described a

‘trickle-down effect’ on youth from professional athletes and teams [20]. Thus, young

impressionable athletes are more likely to abuse SARMs if their favorite athletes and social
 media influencers abuse SARMs. In a cross-sectional randomized response technique survey,

2.7% of young male gym-goers (N = 2264, 24 ± 6 years) reported SARMs use, and 9% reported

using anabolic androgenic steroids [21]. Illegal substance use is commonly underreported, and

Google Search trends analytics indicate that SARMs’ interest is rapidly increasing, and at an all-

time high [22]. Thus, true athlete and gym-goer SARMs use prevalence is likely higher than
                                                                                   T
previously reported (>2.7%). [21]
                                                                            IP
                                                                       R
                                                            SC
In the USA, SARMs are classified as research chemicals that can be legally bought and sold

online; however, marketing SARMs for human consumption is illegal by law. Ironically,

                                                       U
numerous YouTube videos support consumption and describe different ways to properly dose


                                            AN
and cycle SARMs, while hiding behind disclaimers of ‘for entertainment purposes only.’ The top

100 keyword tagged ‘SARMs’ videos on YouTube sorted by relevance add up to over

                                      M
14,000,000 views. Hahamyan et al. [2022] noted that prior to the popular video sharing platform


                              D
TikTok ban of SARMs-related keywords, videos tagged with keyword SARMs totaled more than


                    TE
115 million views [23]. The paucity of clinical research on safe dosing for SARMs and

respective side effects in recreational use suggest users and athletes turn to anecdotal evidence

          EP
from online forums and now YouTube videos for guidance [22, 24].


    C
Alarmingly, YouTube content creators can post videos without review. Thus, YouTube can be a

AC
source of widespread and readily available health misinformation, including celebratory/do-it-

yourself videos on SARMs use. In fact, over 93% of adults in the United States use the internet,

and 8 in 10 online inquiries for health or medical information start at a generic search engine [25,

26]. Many patients/viewers feel that online medical information is the ‘same as’ or ‘better than’
 information from their doctors [27]. Clearly, to understand SARMs abuse, growing social media

content must be analyzed.



The aim of this study is to analyze the: (1) quality; (2) educational content; and (3) reliability of

the most relevant YouTube videos on SARMs to explain growing SARMs abuse by recreational
                                                                                      T
                                                                              IP
and professional sports athletes. Since YouTube video content is not subject to review before

being published, the authors hypothesized that the video quality and reliability would be low, and
                                                                         R
                                                              SC
the educational content would be limited with a bias towards SARMs use.


Materials and Methods

Search/Analysis Strategy
                                                        U
                                             AN
On November 28th, 2021, a cross-sectional analysis of the YouTube video library was

performed. The term ‘SARMs’ was queried on YouTube. The first 100 videos sorted by
                                       M
relevance were recorded. A web scraper was coded using the Beautiful Soup and Selenium

                               D
Python libraries to extract characteristics from the videos. Because these extracted characteristics

                     TE
from YouTube are publicly available, it fulfills criteria for Institutional Review Board (IRB)

exemption, so approval and consent was not required.
          EP
     C
Extracted Characteristics


AC
The following variables were recorded for each video: (1) title; (2) video duration (minutes); (3)

number of views; (4) days since upload; (5) channel name; (6) number of comments; (7) video

tags (descriptive keywords assigned to the video upon upload); (8) view ratio (views/day); (9)

subscriber count; (10) number of likes; (11) number of dislikes; (12) like ratio (number of likes *

100)/(number of likes + number of dislikes); and (13) Video Power Index (VPI). VPI is defined
 as (like ratio * view ratio / 100) and has been characterized in prior literature as a quantitative

measure of video popularity [28-30]. Unique case-insensitive tags were recorded for the 100

videos. Analysis was then restricted to tags that appeared in 4+ videos, and similar tags were

then combined into relevant categories. These tag categories were then used for frequency

analysis and were included in multivariate regressions.
                                                                                      T
Video Categorization
                                                                              IP
                                                                         R
                                                              SC
Two reviewing authors independently reviewed and analyzed all 100 videos. Any discrepancies

of subjective measures were resolved by discussion between the two reviewing authors to remain

uniform.                                                U
                                             AN
Videos were classified based on upload source into the following categories: (1) physician, (2)

                                       M
non-physician, (3) academic, (4) athletic trainer, (5) commercial, and (6) patient. ‘Physician’

videos were uploaded by a physician with an MD or DO degree; ‘nonphysician’ videos were
                               D
                     TE
uploaded by non-physician healthcare providers; ‘academic’ videos were uploaded by authors

Discussion                                  AN
This is the first study to quantitatively analyze YouTube SARMs videos for content, quality, and
                                      M
reliability. Google Search trends analytics suggest that SARMs’ search interest is at an all-time

                              D
high, which is consistent with the primary finding that mean views/video was 147,994 (total

                    TE
views for 100 videos: 14,799,400) [22]. Mean views and VPI for SARMs videos are higher than

nearly all orthopedic and sports medicine YouTube video analyses to date, even despite large
          EP
sample size (n=100) [28-30, 35-42]. Our findings are consistent with previous studies that

    C
demonstrate significant levels of engagement with online medical information [43-45].


AC
The videos analyzed in this study revealed low educational quality and low reliability of

information regarding SARMs. Mean JAMA (1.6) and mean GQS (2.5) scores were consistent

with previous literature suggesting that health information YouTube videos are of low

educational quality and content [28-30, 35-42, 46-48]. Since the VPI differences by source
 categorization, content categorization, and SARMs specific content scores were not statistically

significant, SARMs videos were equally popular by assigned labels validating our methods and

demonstrating that categories were chosen fairly.



Although JAMA scores were consistently low regardless of source or content categorization,
                                                                                  T
                                                                           IP
GQS scores had significant differences by source and content categorization indicating certain

SARMs videos are of higher educational quality. Videos by athletic trainers are of higher
                                                                     R
                                                           SC
educational quality than patient videos (GQS: 2.947, 2.105, p < 0.01), and videos categorized as

general SARMs information were of higher educational quality than videos categorized as user

                                                      U
experience (GQS: 2.722, 1.923, p < 0.05). One explanation is that videos labeled as patient, user

usage and thus present biased views about SARMs usage. This bias is supported by the

more positive in attitude than commercial videos (p < 0.05) and had the highest percentage of

          EP

    C
Potential for propagation of SARMs misinformation is supported by biased anecdotal evidence,

AC
the high mean views compared to other health information YouTube videos, low educational

quality and reliability scores, and the lack of peer-reviewed clinical guidelines for SARMs.

Nearly half (47%) of all SARMs videos analyzed provide specific cycle support, which indicates

that 19.5% of COVID-19 YouTube videos contained nonfactual information, totaling 62,042,609

views [32]. Through tags and its data mining algorithms, YouTube recommends similar content

    C

AC
Conclusion/Summary

SARMs abuse is undoubtedly growing and likely caused by biased and low educational quality

social media misinformation. YouTube SARMs video content, reliability, and educational

quality were poor regardless of source and content categorizations as evidenced by the low mean
 JAMA and GQS scores. Due to the lack of clinical guidelines, safety profiles, and peer-reviewed

literature on SARMs use, there exists an abundance of anecdotal SARMs information. Social

media can be a compelling source of education, but misinformation is abundant. Public health

oversight bodies, clinicians and sports team members must be aware of the social media

misinformation surrounding PEDs to promote discussion and prevent abuse.

 "id":"Q85",
 "sourceFile":"Solving Heat Stress in Sport- Intermittent Cold Air Exposure Mitigates Deterioration of the Autonomic Nervous System in American Football Athletes.pdf",
 "decision":"INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason":"",
 "degradedReason":"",
 "doiMissing":false,
 "identityCheck":"Title in text 'Solving Heat Stress in Sport: Intermittent Cold Air Exposure Mitigates Deterioration of the Autonomic Nervous System in American Football Athletes' matches the filename.",
 "confidence":"medium",
 "studyDesign":"Cohort Study",
 "primaryDomain":"Recovery & Readiness",
 "domains":["Recovery & Readiness","Sports Medicine & Injury"],
 "audiences":["Performance","Athletic Training","Sports Medicine"],
 "sports":["American Football"],
 "populations":["Male Athletes","Collegiate","Healthy Athletes"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Prospective cohort analysis of 50 Division I male football players in the 2023 season who had about 45 to 60 minutes of air-conditioned exposure before training and a 5-minute indoor break during each session, compared with 50 players in 2022 who had no cooling. The 2023 group trained longer (187.4 vs 161.1 min) and spent less time at 38°C or higher (9.7 vs 19.5 min) and 39°C or higher (0.9 vs 10.5 min), and within 2023 time above those thresholds was not associated with next-day heart rate or heart rate variability measures.",
 "screeningLimitations":"The control is a separate, earlier season with no concurrent comparison, and the cold-air arm could not be split into pre-cooling and per-cooling effects. Skin temperature and hydration were not measured, and the sample is one male collegiate team in one hot climate.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff may read the null next-day autonomic result as proof that cold air prevents autonomic decline, when the cooled and uncooled groups came from different seasons.",
 "paper":{
  "year":2025,
  "citation":"Renaghan E, Wishon MJ, Wittels HL, Hecocks D, Galasso PJ, Ren T, et al. Solving Heat Stress in Sport: Intermittent Cold Air Exposure Mitigates Deterioration of the Autonomic Nervous System in American Football Athletes. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise. 2025.",
  "doi":"10.1249/MSS.0000000000003686",
  "abstract":"Objectives: To test whether intermittent cold air exposure weakens the link between training duration, elevated core temperature and next-day autonomic nervous system (ANS) changes in collegiate football players. Methods: Fifty Division I male athletes in 2023 had cold air exposure before and during training. Baseline heart rate, heart rate recovery and heart rate variability were measured 24 hours later and compared with the 2022 season without cooling. Results: The 2023 cohort trained longer, spent less time at 38°C and 39°C or higher, and showed no significant association between training duration and ANS measures at those thresholds. Conclusions: Cold air exposure during training in high heat and humidity may mitigate heat-related ANS deterioration.",
  "tldr":"In collegiate football players training in heat and humidity, cold-air exposure before and during practice cut time at 38°C and 39°C or higher, and next-day autonomic measures did not show the decline seen in the previous season. The comparison is across two seasons, so the result is promising rather than proven.",
  "methods":"Prospective cohort analysis. The 2023 season (50 athletes, 128 sessions) included two cold-air exposures per session, about 45 to 60 minutes before and a 5-minute break during training, and was compared with the 2022 season (50 athletes, no cooling). Core temperature was recorded during training with an armband monitor, and morning baseline heart rate, 30-second heart rate recovery, rMSSD and SDNN were recorded 24 hours after training. Linear regressions were run within each cohort at 37, 38 and 39°C thresholds.",
  "findings":"The 2023 cohort trained longer (187.4 vs 161.1 min) and spent less time at 38°C or higher (9.7 vs 19.5 min) and 39°C or higher (0.9 vs 10.5 min), but more time at 37°C or higher (52.5 vs 30.4 min, marked significant in Table 1). Next-day rMSSD (82.1 vs 72.0 ms) and SDNN (125.6 vs 106.7 ms) were higher in 2023, while baseline heart rate and heart rate recovery were similar. In 2023 time above 38°C and 39°C was not associated with any ANS measure (all p of 0.68 or higher), whereas in 2022 the same associations were significant.",
  "limitations":"The control is a separate season, not a concurrent group, and the cold-air arm could not be split into pre-cooling only or per-cooling only groups. Skin temperature and hydration were not measured, and time at 37°C or higher was higher in 2023, which the text does not discuss. The sample is one male collegiate team in Florida, and five authors are paid employees of Tiger Tech Solutions, which owns the monitor used.",
  "practicalImplications":"Where an air-conditioned facility exists, a cold-air warm-up and a mid-practice cold-air break may be worth trialling in hot, humid football practice, since time at 38°C and above fell. The study cannot say whether pre-cooling or the mid-session break did the work, so track core temperature during any trial.",
  "athleteDev":"For football staff, the cold-air plan was linked to longer practices with less time above 38°C and 39°C, which helps plan heat exposure. The next-day autonomic result is a comparison across seasons, not a controlled effect.",
  "rtp":"Cannot inform return to sport. The cohort was healthy players in training, with no injured athletes and no return-to-play outcome. Its relevance to heat management during rehabilitation sessions in hot conditions was not tested."
 }
}

935	interventions. Third, core temperature and ANS deterioration were estimated using the WFM
936	
937	
938	
939	
940	                          TE
941	which used electrocardiography and infrared temperature technology, both previously validated
942	
943	against their respective gold standard methodologies. Fourth, the study was implemented in a
944	
945	natural setting strengthening the translation of these findings to other sport programs. The current
946	
947	study also has limitations. First, although the comparative cohort was similar, the study did not
948	
949	implement the intervention groups simultaneously, increasing variability in other possible
950	
951	             C
952	confounding factors. Second, our study design did not include a pre-cooling only or per-cooling
953	
954	only group, as such, conclusions on the independent effect of each cooling interval cannot be
955	
956	  C
957	drawn. Third, because skin temperature was not measured, we are unable observe any changes in
958	
959	
960	
961	A
962	the core: skin temperature gradients. Fourth, this study was conducted in one sample of male,
963	
964	collegiate American football athletes from one geographical location and as such, our
965	
966	observations may not be generalizable to other sports and/or female athletes. Lastly, the
967	
968	hydration and nutrition status of the athletes were not measured.
969	 CONCLUSIONS
970	
971	       The findings of the current study demonstrate the potential effectiveness of cold air
972	
973	exposure mitigating the precipitous increase in core temperature and subsequent deterioration of
974	
975	the ANS. Specifically, athletes exposed to 45 to 60 minutes of cold air prior to and during a
976	
977	single, 5-minute rest interval while training outdoors in high heat and humidity decreased the
978	
979	time spent training at elevated core temperature thresholds (≥ 38°C and ≥ 39°C). Moreover, the
980	
981	
982	                                                                D
983	athletes, on average, did not exhibit signs of ANS deterioration unlike our former study. The
984	
985	current study uniquely identified an effective cooling strategy that may help prevent deterioration
986	
987	
988	
989	
990	                        EP
991	of the ANS in collegiate, American football athletes, allowing coaching staff to safely train their
992	
993	athletes during seasons with high heat and humidity. We strongly recommend that future studies
994	
995	
996	
997	
998	                          TE
999	evaluate the effectiveness of existing cooling intervention methods in American football. Further,
1000	
1001	for the cold air method, researchers should explore different durations and frequencies to
1002	
1003	determine the most effective cold air exposure.

 INTRODUCTION

       Exercise-induced heat stress, if prolonged and without reprieve, imposes detrimental

effects on physiological functions, many of which are regulated by the autonomic nervous

system (ANS) (1–3). Research shows that slight increases in core temperature (> 1°C) may

induce ANS deterioration that progressively worsens with exposure time, especially when

exercising in a hot and humid environment (4). For American football athletes, maintaining


                                                                 D
physiologically tolerable and safe core temperatures is exceptionally challenging given their

heat-resistant uniforms, larger body masses and long duration practices (~2 to 4 hours) (5–7).




                        EP
Thus, finding cooling interventions that effectively mitigate the precipitous increase in core

temperature as previously observed in athletes, is imperative for preventing perturbations to ANS




                          TE
function and exertional heat-related illnesses.



       Extensive research previously evaluated the effectiveness of different cooling strategies

on exercise-induced heat stress in athletes (8–10). Internal and external cooling methodologies

were tested including but not limited to cold water or ice ingestion, menthol spray, peripheral and

             C
whole-body cold water or ice water immersion, ice garments, moving air (i.e., fan), and cold air

exposure (8). Athletes utilized these methods either independently or in combination at different

  C
time points relative to their practice or competition (e.g., pre-cooling, per-cooling, post-cooling)



A
(11). Collectively, the evidence suggests that pre-cooling using the whole-body cold water

immersion method (CWI) is most effective in lowering skin and core temperatures, subsequently

curtailing accelerated increases in core temperature during training in high heat and humidity.

While effective, the CWI method is impractical as it is time- and resource-intensive for large

teams like American football (n~80 to 100 athletes). Additionally, few studies exist among non-
 endurance sports and sports that require athletes to wear heat-trapping uniforms. Thus, cooling

interventions successfully mitigating large increases in core temperature while training in high

heat and humidity and preventing deterioration of ANS function remains unclear for sports like

American football (7). Our previous work demonstrated the negative influence of elevated core

temperatures on ANS function 24 hours post training. During training, athletes reaching a

minimum core temperature of 38.0°C showed deterioration of the ANS, reflected by higher


                                                                   D
baseline heart rates (HR), slower HR recovery post-acute exercise and lower HR variability.(4)




                         EP
       Many collegiate American football programs, especially those located in hot and humid

geographical locations like the southeastern United States, are likely equipped with adequately




                           TE
sized, air-conditioned training facilities. Interestingly, cold air exposure as a cooling strategy, for

any sport, is extremely limited in the scientific literature (12). Like CWI, cooling via air-

conditioning exposes a large proportion of an athlete’s body surface area to cooler air, facilitating

reductions in skin and core temperatures. Quite possibly, a cold air intervention prior to and

during training may successfully temper the accelerated increase in core temperature, allowing

             C
athletes to train longer in high heat and humidity without adversely affecting ANS function and

augmenting the risk of heat injuries (13). To our knowledge, no studies previously evaluated the

  C
effects of intermittent cold air exposure on ANS function in American football. Therefore, the



A
current study investigated the effects of an intermittent cold air exposure on the association

between training duration, core temperature thresholds, and ANS recovery. We hypothesized that

the cold air exposure would mitigate the heat-related increase in core temperature, allowing

athletes to train longer in high heat and humidity without inducing ANS deterioration 24 hours

post training.
 MATERIALS AND METHODS

Study Design

       The current study analyzed data from a prospective cohort that examined ANS function

of Division I collegiate American football athletes during and 24 hours post exercise training

throughout two, 27-week seasons (2022 and 2023). Baseline HR, HR recovery and HR

variability were measured as indicators of ANS function and were measured only during the

weeks the athletes trained (n=25).

country. Two authors are members of a marginalized community. Our study population included

male athletes from different socioeconomic backgrounds and minority groups participating in

collegiate American Football academies; thus, findings may not be generalizable to settings with

fewer resources.

The exercise training sessions (n=128) lasted, on average, 161.1 (40.6.) min and 187.4 (43.1)

min for the 2022 and 2023 cohorts, respectively. All athletes were exposed to the same training

which varied in intensity and exercises performed within and between sessions. Training

 C

strength- and power-focused resistive exercises, short-distance sprint intervals, aerobic training,

        Historical weather data for the 2022 and 2023 seasons (May through November) were

obtained from the National Weather Service (National Atmospheric and Oceanic Administration

from 26.1°C to 29.6°C with a minimum and maximum temperature of 22.4°C and 33.2°C,

from 25.4°C to 30.0°C with a minimum and maximum temperature of 21.9°C and 34.4°C,

Cold Air Exposure Intervention. Whole-body cold air exposure was implemented during the

2023 season (May to November) and was used as the cooling intervention method and was

incorporated twice during each training session. The cold air was delivered via an air-

conditioned, indoor practice facility (90,000 ft2) on the university’s campus. The air conditioning

system was set at 15.6℃. The first exposure occurred at the beginning of the training session

             C
where athletes performed their warmup routines and sport-specific drills for 45 to 60 minutes.

Following, the athletes moved to the outdoor training facility and engaged in 30 to 45 minutes of

 C
exercise. A 5-minute break inside the air-conditioned facility occurred immediately after training



A
outdoors. Here, athletes only removed their helmets, then rested, and performed no additional

exercises. Athletes then returned outdoors for an additional 30-minute training session.



Physiological Measurements. Throughout each training session, participants wore armband

monitors that continuously measured core temperature, HR, and indices of HRV (Warfighter
 Monitor (WFM), Tiger Tech Solutions Inc., Miami, FL, USA). The WFM is equipped with

several biometric capabilities including but not limited to temperature sensor and

electrocardiography and was previously validated in many subpopulations, including athletes (4,

14, 15). The monitors were secured on the upper left arm with an elastic band encompassing the

widest part of the biceps muscle. Monitors were worn prior to and throughout each training

session.


                                                                   D
Core Temperature. Core body temperature was derived from temperature sensors on the WFM.




                           EP
The temperature sensors on the WFM are medical-grade infrared temperature sensors which

have been calibrated to core body temperature across thousands of subjects in a hospital setting




                             TE
utilizing health monitors and Swan–Ganz catheters as the gold standard measure(16, 17). Core

temperature was measured throughout the duration of each training session.



24 h ANS Recovery and Function. The current study used electrocardiogram-based metrics to

represent ANS recovery and function given that cardiac activity is a strong indicator of ANS

             C
activity. The release of     acetylcholine and epinephrine from cardiac nerve fibers controls the

firing rate of the sinoatrial (SA) node affecting cardiac activity (18, 19). Thus, cardiac metrics

  C
like baseline HR, HR recovery and heart rate variability (HRV) provide accurate information on



A
the interaction between parasympathetic and sympathetic nervous systems, the two branches of

the ANS.



Baseline HR. Baseline HR represented ANS recovery and was measured in the morning (0600–

0700), prior to the start of a football training session and 24 h after the start of the previous day’s
 training session. Baseline HR was obtained following at least 4 min of inactivity, per established

protocols (20). During this measurement, all athletes remained seated and nearly motionless for 5

min to collect a “resting” baseline HR.



HR Recovery. HR recovery was measured throughout the next day’s football training session, 24

h following the previous day’s training session. HR recovery was defined as the reduction in HR


                                                                D
during 30 s rest intervals and represented localized parasympathetic activation. HR recovery was

measured within the first 30 s of the rest interval, as during this period HR exhibits the greatest




                         EP
rate of change following an acute bout of exercise (21). HR recovery was estimated during all

rest intervals occurring within a training session and then averaged.




                           TE
HRV. Like baseline HR, HRV was measured in the morning (0600–0700), prior to the start of a

football training session and 24 h after the start of the previous day’s training session. Per

established protocols (20), HRV was obtained following at least 4 min of inactivity. During this

time, all athletes remained seated and nearly motionless for 5 min to collect a “resting” HRV

             C
measure. Two HRV time-domain indices were measured which assessed the changes in the inter-

beat interval including RR and NN intervals. RR intervals were the time between R waves on

  C
consecutive QRS complexes and NN intervals were noise-free RR intervals. From these data, the



A
two separate time-domain indices were derived including SDNN (standard deviation of the NN

interval) and RMSSD (the root mean square of the standard deviation of the NN interval). These

HRV time-domain indices have been shown to reflect parasympathetic autonomic output

(rMSSD and SDNN) and sympathetic output (SDNN) (18) and are more robust to external

stimuli like respiration cycles(22, 23).
        Because the current study focused on ANS recovery and function 24 h post-exercise

training, baseline HR, HR recovery and HRV were not measured following one or more rest

days. For example, baseline HR, HR recovery and HRV were not measured on Mondays during

summer training camps as this day was preceded by two rest days (Saturday and Sunday). The

inclusion of rest days in the analyses would likely weaken the associations and, thus, less

accurately estimate the acute impact of exercise training.

temperature thresholds with and without whole-body cold air exposure prior to and during acute

exercise. The cooling method, duration (in minutes) of exercise training and core temperature

(℃served as the primary independent variables. 24-hr HR and HRV indices (SDNN and

rMSSD), and HR recovery served as the primary outcome variables and represented ANS

recovery and function within 24h post-exercise training, respectively. The associations between

             C

DISCUSSION

       The current study investigated the effects of two intermittent cooling sessions via cold air


                                                                D
exposure on the association between training duration, core temperature thresholds, and ANS

recovery. We hypothesized that the cold air exposure would mitigate the heat-related increase in




                       EP
core temperature, allowing athletes to train longer in high heat and humidity outdoors without

inducing ANS deterioration 24 hours post training. The major finding of this study was that




                         TE
athletes enduring a cold air exposure prior to and during exercise training in high heat and

humidity nullified the association between training duration, elevated core temperatures, and

ANS deterioration 24 hours post-exercise training. The null relationships observed were likely

consequent to athletes spending considerably less time training under the higher core temperature

thresholds (≥ 38°C and ≥ 39°C), allowing athletes to train for longer durations without

            C
negatively affecting ANS function the next day. Our observations may suggest that providing

athletes intermittent exposures to cold air of sufficient duration may mitigate the rise in core

 C
temperature consequent to prolonged exercise training in hot and humid climates and alleviate



A
any associated negative effects on ANS recovery and function.



       The most novel aspect of the current study was that the cold air exposure appeared to

nullify the association between training duration in high heat and humidity, elevated core

temperatures, and 24-hour ANS deterioration. Specifically, athletes exposed to cold air prior to
 and during exercise trainings sessions in a hot and humid climate, did not exhibit decrements in

baseline HR, HR recovery or HRV 24 hours post exercise training, despite expected heat-related

increases in core temperature. These observations starkly contrast our recently published work

that explored the relationships between prolonged exercise training duration in high heat and

humidity and ANS recovery and function (see tables 2-3) (4). In that study, the athletes

performed similar practice sessions with respect to duration and exercise training regimen. The


                                                               D
athletes, however, were not exposed to any cooling method prior to, during or following each

training session. Not surprisingly, significant associations between exercise training duration,




                       EP
under specific core temperature thresholds, and ANS recovery and function were observed. At

the higher core temperature thresholds (≥ 38°C and ≥ 39°C), athletes experienced higher baseline




                         TE
HRs, slower HR recovery during rest intervals and impaired HRV indicating significant

deterioration of the ANS 24 hours post training. Thus, the observation of the current study in

addition to our previous study suggest that the cold air exposure method may mitigate the

negative influences of prolonged exercise training in high heat and humidity on the ANS (24–

26).

            C
       The null associations observed may be explained by the athletes spending considerably

 C
less time training under the higher core temperature thresholds, despite longer overall training



A
duration, relative to the 2022 cohort (≥ 38°C: 19.5 min vs 9.7 min; ≥ 39°C: 10.5 min vs 0.9 min,

respectively). This finding suggests that cold air exposure, of sufficient duration, may augment

an athlete’s heat storage capacity (9, 27). Current evidence implicates that the gradient between

core temperature and skin temperature (core: skin) strongly influences an individual’s

thermoregulatory response to exercising in the heat. Specifically, several studies previously
 demonstrated cooling methods that effectively lower skin temperature, and ideally core

temperature, improve exercise performance (e.g., time-to-exhaustion, maximal capacity).

Unfortunately, few studies have evaluated the effectiveness of cold air exposure on skin and core

temperatures, yielding inconsistent findings. However, one cooling strategy, whole-body cold-

water immersion that is like the cold-air exposure method and extensively studied, effectively

lowers skin and core temperatures (27). The cooling of the large skin surface area induces


                                                               D
peripheral vasoconstriction, recirculating colder blood back to the thoracic region, lowering core

temperature and reducing the thermo-physiological strain of exercise training in high heat and




                        EP
humidity. As such, athletes, as shown in the current study and others (8, 27, 28), may perform

exercise in the heat and humidity for longer durations and delaying the onset of heat-related




                          TE
declines in performance. We acknowledge however, that it is also possible that the longer

training durations in the 2023 cohort could be attributed to variation in training regimens and

accounting for transition times between the cooling phases. During these transitions, athletes

(n=100) gathered their gear, regrouped and returned outdoors for additional training.



             C
       Unlike several former studies (13, 29), the current study implemented the cooling method

prior to and during exercise training sessions. Additionally, during the pre-cooling phase, the

 C
athletes were performing low to moderate intensity exercise. This contrasts to many other



A
cooling methods where athletes remain stationary during their pre-cooling exposure which may

be disadvantageous when transitioning to exercise training in high heat and humidity (10, 11).

This method may result in simultaneous increases in core and skin temperature during the onset

of exercise. Consequently, this may accelerate the decrease in the core: skin temperature gradient

and increasing core temperature more quickly. The method used in the current study, however,
 potentially mitigated this response as the athletes were exposed to cold air while simultaneously

exercising. As such, the transition to exercising outdoors in the high heat and humidity may

affect the core: skin temperature gradient to a lesser degree (30, 31) allowing for longer training

duration. Moreover, the mid-session cooling phase (~5 min) implemented following 45 to 60

mins of exercise training outdoors likely slowed the increase in core temperature and narrowing

of the core: skin temperature gradient. This response allowed athletes to perform an additional


                                                                 D
bout of outdoor training, staving off the rapid increase in core and skin temperatures. In support,

athletes in the current study were able to train for longer (187.4 vs 161.1 min) and spent less time




                         EP
under higher elevated core temperatures. Our finding suggests that implementing both cooling

sessions may more effectively mitigate the precipitous increase in core temperature (10, 13)




                           TE
during outdoor training in high heat and humidity.



Practical Implications

       Critically, American football ranks in the top 5 for sports with the highest prevalence of

exertional heat-related illnesses (3), conditions that negatively impact the ANS. Unfortunately,

             C
the evidence base for practical, effective cooling strategies in this sport is extremely limited. As

such, identifying that cold air exposure effectively mitigates the precipitous increase in core

  C
temperature, possibly preventing deterioration of the ANS. This finding profoundly impacts the



A
scientific literature and sports realm. Moreover, this cooling method is significantly less

burdensome compared to other effective methods like cold water immersion and ice garments.

These methods are not conducive to sport-specific movement nor practical application for large

sports teams like American football which includes ≥ 100 athletes on roster. However, the cold
 air exposure method is time efficient and only requires an air-conditioned facility that likely

already exists at most collegiate American football programs.



       The current study has several novel aspects that significantly expand the existing

evidence base. First, we uniquely identified a cooling strategy for collegiate American football

athletes, an understudied subpopulation, that effectively alleviates the previously documented


                                                                 D
ANS deterioration consequent to prolonged exercise training in a hot and humid climate. Second,

the 2022 cohort was similar regarding the demographic and anthropometric athlete profiles,




                        EP
exercise training regimens and climate, allowing for appropriate comparisons between the

interventions. Third, core temperature and ANS deterioration were estimated using the WFM




                          TE
which used electrocardiography and infrared temperature technology, both previously validated

against their respective gold standard methodologies. Fourth, the study was implemented in a

natural setting strengthening the translation of these findings to other sport programs. The current

study also has limitations. First, although the comparative cohort was similar, the study did not

implement the intervention groups simultaneously, increasing variability in other possible

             C
confounding factors. Second, our study design did not include a pre-cooling only or per-cooling

only group, as such, conclusions on the independent effect of each cooling interval cannot be

  C
drawn. Third, because skin temperature was not measured, we are unable observe any changes in



A
the core: skin temperature gradients. Fourth, this study was conducted in one sample of male,

collegiate American football athletes from one geographical location and as such, our

observations may not be generalizable to other sports and/or female athletes. Lastly, the

hydration and nutrition status of the athletes were not measured.
 CONCLUSIONS

       The findings of the current study demonstrate the potential effectiveness of cold air

exposure mitigating the precipitous increase in core temperature and subsequent deterioration of

the ANS. Specifically, athletes exposed to 45 to 60 minutes of cold air prior to and during a

single, 5-minute rest interval while training outdoors in high heat and humidity decreased the

time spent training at elevated core temperature thresholds (≥ 38°C and ≥ 39°C). Moreover, the


                                                                D
athletes, on average, did not exhibit signs of ANS deterioration unlike our former study. The

current study uniquely identified an effective cooling strategy that may help prevent deterioration




                        EP
of the ANS in collegiate, American football athletes, allowing coaching staff to safely train their

athletes during seasons with high heat and humidity. We strongly recommend that future studies




                          TE
evaluate the effectiveness of existing cooling intervention methods in American football. Further,

for the cold air method, researchers should explore different durations and frequencies to

determine the most effective cold air exposure.

import json
d=json.load(open('drafts/Q85.json'))
p=d['paper']
d['evidenceSummary']="Prospective cohort analysis of 50 Division I male football players in the 2023 season who did 45 to 60 minutes of warm-up and drills in an air-conditioned indoor facility (set at 15.6°C) at the start of each session and took a 5-minute indoor break mid-session, compared with 50 players in 2022 who had no cooling. The 2023 group trained longer (187.4 vs 161.1 min) and spent less time at 38°C or higher (9.7 vs 19.5 min) and 39°C or higher (0.9 vs 10.5 min), and within 2023 time above those thresholds was not associated with next-day heart rate or heart rate variability measures."
p['methods']="Prospective cohort analysis. The 2023 season (50 athletes, 128 sessions) included two cold-air exposures per session: 45 to 60 minutes of warm-up and sport-specific drills in an indoor facility air-conditioned to 15.6°C at the start of the session, and a 5-minute seated break indoors after the first outdoor block. It was compared with the 2022 season (50 athletes, no cooling). Core temperature was recorded during training with an armband monitor, morning baseline heart rate, rMSSD and SDNN were recorded about 24 hours after training, 30-second heart rate recovery was taken in the next day's session, and linear regressions were run within each cohort at 37, 38 and 39°C thresholds."
p['limitations']="The control is a separate season, not a concurrent group, the cold-air arm could not be split into pre-cooling only or per-cooling only groups, and the authors note the longer 2023 sessions may partly reflect training variation and transition time. Skin temperature and hydration were not measured, core temperature was estimated by an armband infrared sensor, and time at 37°C or higher was higher in 2023, which the text does not discuss. The sample is one male collegiate team in Florida, and five authors are paid employees of Tiger Tech Solutions, which owns the monitor used."
d['verification']={"status":"CORRECTED","changes":["evidenceSummary and paper.methods: cold-air exposure described as 45 to 60 min 'before training' -> 45 to 60 min of warm-up and drills inside the air-conditioned facility at the start of the session (\"The first exposure occurred at the beginning of the training session where athletes performed their warmup routines and sport-specific drills for 45 to 60 minutes\"); HR recovery timing clarified (measured during next day's session)","paper.limitations: added the authors' caveat that longer 2023 sessions may reflect training variation and transitions (\"longer training durations in the 2023 cohort could be attributed to variation in training regimens\") and the armband-derived core temperature"],"residualConcerns":"Between-season comparison only; 2023 regressions are compared descriptively with previously published 2022 results. Five authors are employees of the monitor's manufacturer.","spotCheckPriority":"high"}
json.dump(d,open('verified/Q85.json','w'),indent=1,ensure_ascii=False)

 "id": "Q86",
 "sourceFile": "South African Institute of Drug-Free Sport Postion Statement on CBD (Cannabidiol) and THC (Tetrahydrocannabinol).pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",

 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Title in text 'South African Institute of Drug-Free Sport Position Statement on CBD (Cannabidiol) and THC (Tetrahydrocannabinol)' matches the filename, apart from the typo 'Postion' in the filename.",
 "confidence": "medium",
 "studyDesign": "Consensus / Position Statement",
 "primaryDomain": "Athlete Wellbeing",
 "domains": [
  "Athlete Wellbeing",
  "Nutrition & Hydration"
 ],
 "audiences": [
  "Sports Medicine",
  "Athletic Training",

 ],
 "sports": [
  "Mixed / General Sport"
 ],
 "populations": [
  "Mixed / Unspecified"
 ],
 "evidenceSummary": "Position statement from the South African Institute for Drug-free Sport, supported by the South African Sports Medicine Association, on CBD and THC in athletes, with no original data. It summarises WADA's 2022 expert group conclusion that THC meets the criteria for the Prohibited List, and notes that the cited CBD and THC studies are of low evidence level, with few randomised trials, small samples and case studies.",
 "screeningLimitations": "A position statement with no described search method and no formal grading of evidence. It reflects an anti-doping viewpoint, and the legal position on cannabis varies by country and is still changing.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read 'CBD is not prohibited' as safe to use before competition, when the statement warns that CBD products can contain THC and cause a positive test.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2023,
  "citation": "Pillay L, Thompson C, Tabane C, Kirby J, Hendricks S, Swart J, et al. South African Institute of Drug-Free Sport Position Statement on CBD (Cannabidiol) and THC (Tetrahydrocannabinol). S Afr J Sports Med. 2023;35(1):1-4.",
  "doi": "10.17159/2078-516X/2023/v35i1a16097",
  "abstract": "Unlabelled opening paragraph: CBD and THC have become easily available to athletes. Using them may expose an athlete to an adverse analytical finding (a positive test) and sanction, especially without a therapeutic use exemption. The statement aims to clarify the use of CBD and THC and their anti-doping risks, and the South African Sports Medicine Association supports it.",
  "tldr": "CBD is not prohibited, but THC is, and a CBD product can contain enough THC to cause a positive test. Athletes should check every product against the Prohibited List and seek a therapeutic use exemption before any medical cannabinoid use.",
  "methods": "Position statement by a national anti-doping body, supported by the national sports medicine association. It reviews WADA rules, South African law, product types and the evidence base, with no original data and no described search method.",
  "findings": "CBD is not on the Prohibited List, while cannabis (THC) is prohibited in competition. WADA's 2022 expert group concluded that THC meets the criteria for the List: it poses health risks, has no objective evidence of physiological performance benefit, and violates the spirit of sport. The urine threshold for an adverse analytical finding is 150 ng/ml, and 180 ng/ml triggers sanction. The statement adds that evidence for CBD and THC in anxiety, pain, sleep disorders and chemotherapy side effects is low in quality.",
  "limitations": "Position statement with no described search method or evidence grading, and the cited studies are mostly small or uncontrolled. It presents an anti-doping viewpoint, and the statement itself says South African cannabis legislation is still being approved in stages. The authors declare no conflicts of interest or funding.",
  "practicalImplications": "Athletes who use CBD should check each product, since some contain THC and a single positive test can bring sanctions. Medicinal cannabinoid use for a diagnosed condition needs a therapeutic use exemption before treatment starts, and evidence-based first-line options should be tried first.",
  "athleteDev": "THC is banned in competition, and WADA's 2022 group found no objective evidence that it enhances physical performance, although neuropsychological effects cannot be excluded. Staff should not treat THC as a performance aid, and should ask about CBD use because its THC content is a doping risk.",
  "rtp": "Limited return-to-sport value because it sets no return-to-play rules. It is relevant only where cannabinoids are used for pain, sleep or nausea during rehabilitation, where a THC-containing product needs a therapeutic use exemption."
 }
}

They trained bench press twice weekly for 8 weeks at 55% to 70% of 1RM, and 1RM rose in the 15%, 25% and 50% groups (all P < .001) but not the 0% group, with the largest rise in the 25% group (68.0 to 78.8 kg).",
 "screeningLimitations":"The participants were resistance-trained but not athletes, and the study used one exercise, 8 weeks and a single ultrasound slice for muscle size. The abstract says participants were randomly assigned, but the Methods describe allocation by 1RM with ABBA counterbalancing, so the allocation method is unclear.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read the 25% threshold as a universal best setting, but most between-group gains did not differ and the advantage lies in effect sizes, in non-athletes doing bench press only.",

  "year":2022,
  "citation":"Rodiles-Guerrero L, Cornejo-Daza PJ, Sánchez-Valdepeñas J, Alcazar J, Rodriguez-López C, Sánchez-Moreno M, et al. Specific Adaptations to 0%, 15%, 25%, and 50% Velocity-Loss Thresholds During Bench Press Training. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2022.",
  "doi":"10.1123/ijspp.2021-0481",
  "abstract":"Purpose: To compare four velocity-loss (VL) thresholds (0%, 15%, 25% and 50%) on strength, neuromuscular adaptations and muscle hypertrophy during bench press at 55% to 70% of 1RM. Methods: Fifty resistance-trained men were assigned to four groups for an 8-week, 16-session program that differed in the VL allowed per set. Results: A group by time interaction for 1RM (P = .01) showed gains in all groups except VL0, with the largest gains in VL25; only VL25 increased pectoralis EMG, and only VL50 increased pectoralis cross-sectional area. Conclusions: A VL threshold of about 25% optimised strength and neuromuscular adaptations, while higher thresholds promoted hypertrophy.",
  "tldr":"Eight weeks of bench press at 55% to 70% of 1RM with a 25% velocity-loss cutoff gave the largest 1RM gains, while the 50% cutoff was the only setting that increased chest muscle size. Choose the cutoff to match the goal, and remember the sample was not athletes.",
  "methods":"Four groups of resistance-trained men trained bench press twice weekly for 8 weeks, with three sets per session at a set load (55% to 70% of 1RM) and a velocity-loss cutoff of 0%, 15%, 25% or 50% per set. Outcomes were pectoralis cross-sectional area by ultrasound, isometric force and EMG, a progressive loading test with 1RM, and a fatigue test, measured 72 hours before and after training.",
  "findings":"1RM rose in the 15%, 25% and 50% groups (P < .001) but not the 0% group (group by time P = .01), with the largest rise in the 25% group (68.0 to 78.8 kg). Pectoralis cross-sectional area rose only in the 50% group (P < .001), with no group by time interaction. Pectoralis EMG rose only in the 25% group (group by time P = .03), and triceps EMG fell only in the 50% group (P = .006). Isometric force rose in all groups, and most between-group differences in gains were not significant.",
  "limitations":"Participants were resistance-trained men, not athletes, and the study covered one exercise, 8 weeks, and one ultrasound slice for muscle size. Randomisation is unclear, as the abstract says random assignment but the Methods describe ABBA counterbalancing by 1RM.",
  "practicalImplications":"For bench press at 55% to 70% of 1RM, a 25% velocity-loss cutoff per set looks best for strength and pectoral activation, while a 50% cutoff was the only setting that grew chest size, with lower triceps activity. The authors advise against going beyond a moderate loss, because extra repetitions may not help strength.",
  "athleteDev":"The results come from resistance-trained non-athletes, so they should inform strength planning for athletes with caution. The study used a linear velocity transducer, so velocity-loss cutoffs need monitoring equipment, and it does not test athletes or other lifts.",
  "rtp":"Not applicable to return to sport. The sample was healthy resistance-trained men, and no injury or rehabilitation outcome was measured."
 }
}

      Speciﬁc Adaptations to 0%, 15%, 25%, and 50% Velocity-Loss
               Thresholds During Bench Press Training
             Luis Rodiles-Guerrero,1,2 Pedro Jesús Cornejo-Daza,1,2 Juan Sánchez-Valdepeñas,1,2
         Julian Alcazar,3,4 Carlos Rodriguez-López,3,4 Miguel Sánchez-Moreno,5 Luis María Alegre,3,4
                            Juan A. León-Prados,1,2 and Fernando Pareja-Blanco1,2
         1
          Physical Performance & Sports Research Center, Department of Sports and Computer Sciences, Universidad Pablo de Olavide, Seville, Spain;
           2
             Faculty of Sport Sciences, Department of Sports and Computer Sciences, Universidad Pablo de Olavide, Seville, Spain; 3GENUD Toledo
              Research Group, Universidad de Castilla-La Mancha, Toledo, Spain; 4CIBER of Frailty and Healthy Aging (CIBERFES), Madrid, Spain;
                                        5
                                         Department of Physical Education and Sports, University of Seville, Seville, Spain

     Purpose: To compare the effect of 4 velocity-loss (VL) thresholds—0% (VL0), 15% (VL15), 25% (VL25), and 50% (VL50)—
     on strength gains, neuromuscular adaptations, and muscle hypertrophy during the bench press (BP) exercise using intensities
     ranging from 55% to 70% of 1-repetition maximum (1RM). Methods: Fifty resistance-trained men were randomly assigned to 4
     groups that followed an 8-week (16 sessions) BP training program at 55% to 70% 1RM but differed in the VL allowed in each set
     (VL0, VL15, VL25, and VL50). Assessments performed before (pre) and after (post) the training program included (1) cross-
     sectional area of pectoralis major muscle, (2) maximal isometric test, (3) progressive loading test, and (4) fatigue test in the BP
     exercise. Results: A signiﬁcant group × time interaction was found for 1RM (P = .01), where all groups except VL0 showed
     signiﬁcant gains in 1RM strength (P < .001). The VL25 group attained the greatest gains in 1RM strength and most load–velocity
     relationship parameters analyzed. A signiﬁcant group × time interaction was observed for EMG root mean square in pectoralis
     major (P = .03) where only the VL25 group showed signiﬁcant increases (P = .02). VL50 showed decreased EMG root mean
     square in triceps brachii (P = .006). Only the VL50 group showed signiﬁcant increases in cross-sectional area (P < .001).
     Conclusions: These ﬁndings indicate that a VL threshold of about 25% with intensities from 55% to 70% 1RM in BP provides an
     optimal training stimulus to maximize dynamic strength performance and neuromuscular adaptations, while higher VL
     thresholds promote higher muscle hypertrophy.

     Keywords: resistance training, velocity-based training, training volume, muscle strength, neuromuscular, muscle hypertrophy
